value.title: Introduction to Stylistics
value.description: Foundational concepts of linguistic choices and their impact on audience perception.

lessons.title: What is Stylistics?
lessons.subtitle: The study of linguistic choices and their aesthetic effects.

content.heading: Core Definition
content.body: Stylistics: The study of the distinctive linguistic features of a text, exploring how language choices shape meaning and effect.

content.heading: Overview
content.body: Stylistics sits at the intersection of linguistics and literary criticism. It provides tools to describe systematically how writers use language to create meaning and achieve effects.

content.quote: Style is the dress of thought.

lessons.title: Foregrounding & Deviation
lessons.subtitle: How language draws attention to itself.

content.heading: Core Definition
content.body: Foregrounding: A linguistic technique that makes a text stand out by departing from ordinary expected language use.

content.heading: Types of Foregrounding
content.body: Foregrounding occurs through two main processes: deviation (breaking linguistic rules) and parallelism (creating structured repetition). Both draw the reader's attention to the form of the text itself.

content.heading: Case Analysis: e.e. cummings
content.body: The poet e.e. cummings systematically foregrounded his texts through graphic deviation â€” refusing to capitalize proper nouns, fragmenting syntax, and playing with spatial layout on the page.

steps.label: Graphological Deviation
steps.body: Non-standard capitalization and punctuation break reader expectations.

steps.label: Syntactic Deviation
steps.body: Unusual word order forces slow, deliberate reading.

value.title: Figurative Language
value.description: Mastering metaphor, metonymy, and the cognitive structures of imagery.

lessons.title: The Art of the Metaphor
lessons.subtitle: Transcending literal meaning to forge profound connections between disparate ideas.

content.heading: Core Definition
content.body: Metaphor: A figure of speech in which a word or phrase is applied to an object or action to which it is not literally applicable.

content.heading: Beyond the Comparison
content.body: Unlike the simile, which acknowledges the comparison using 'like' or 'as', the metaphor asserts an identity between the subjects. It is an act of linguistic courage, claiming that one thing is another to illuminate a hidden quality or shared essence.

content.imageAlt: A macro photograph of an antique clockwork mechanism inside a polished silver pocket watch, representing the metaphor 'time is a machine'. Dramatic lighting highlights intricate brass gears.
content.quote: "The metaphor is perhaps one of man's most fruitful potentialities. Its efficacy verges on magic."

content.heading: Case Analysis: Shakespeare's Stage
content.body: Consider the famous line from As You Like It: "All the world's a stage."

steps.label: The Vehicle
steps.body: The 'Stage' represents the structure of human life, implying that our actions are performative and transitory.

steps.label: The Tenor
steps.body: The 'World' is the actual subject being described, reimagined through the lens of theatrical artifice.

lessons.title: Simile & Analogy
lessons.subtitle: Drawing explicit comparisons to illuminate hidden truths.

content.heading: Core Definition
content.body: Simile: A figure of speech that directly compares two things using the words 'like', 'as', 'than', or 'resembles'.

content.heading: Simile vs Metaphor
content.body: While the metaphor boldly asserts identity ('Life is a journey'), the simile hedges with a marker of comparison ('Life is like a journey'). This subtle difference carries enormous rhetorical weight â€” the simile invites analysis, the metaphor demands acceptance.

content.quote: "My love is like a red, red rose."

lessons.title: Metonymy & Synecdoche
lessons.subtitle: The art of substitution in language.

content.heading: Core Definition
content.body: Metonymy: A figure of speech in which a thing is referred to by the name of something closely associated with it (e.g., 'The Crown' for the monarchy).

content.heading: Metonymy in Daily Speech
content.body: Metonymy is deeply embedded in everyday language. When we say 'Washington decided', we use 'Washington' (the city) to stand for the US government. This substitution compresses complex ideas into memorable, evocative shorthand.

content.heading: Synecdoche: Part for Whole
content.body: Synecdoche is a special type of metonymy where a part represents the whole, or vice versa.

steps.label: Part for Whole
steps.body: 'All hands on deck' â€” 'hands' stand for sailors.

steps.label: Whole for Part
steps.body: 'England won the match' â€” 'England' stands for the English team.

lessons.title: Enallage
lessons.subtitle: The deliberate substitution of grammatical forms for rhetorical effect.

content.heading: Core Definition
content.body: Enallage: The deliberate substitution of one grammatical form for another, often involving a shift in person, number, case, gender, or tense for rhetorical effect.

content.heading: Linguistic Function
content.body: In poetry, it disrupts the expected rhythm to force the reader's attention onto specific emotional shifts. In prose, it mimics natural speech patterns or characterizes a speaker's social standing or psychological state.
